Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Arthur has always considered himself a private, cautious man. At seventy-one, he has cultivated a life of quiet routine, one he believed was built on prudence rather than fear. Yet, sitting in the therapist’s office, he admits that the walls he has built around himself have become a prison. For over sixty years, a part of him has remained a terrified eight-year-old boy, trapped in the dim, narrow hallway of his childhood home. The memory is not a story he tells himself, but a series of fragments that ambush him. Sometimes, it’s just a flash of the faded floral wallpaper. Other times, the memory arrives as a smell, so potent it eclipses the present moment: the sharp, sour scent of whiskey on his father’s breath. These flashes feel more real and vivid to Arthur than the memory of what he ate for breakfast; they are not memories of the past, but events happening now.

The event that seeded this lifelong vigilance was one of many similar nights. His father, a man made unpredictable and cruel by drink, had been enraged that Arthur had been seen talking to a new neighbor. As his father cornered him in the hallway, the smell of alcohol was overwhelming. Through the thin walls, Arthur heard the distant wail of a siren and a desperate, childish hope flared in his chest—that someone would come, someone would see. But the sound faded down the street, leaving him alone. The punishment was swift and silent, followed by a hissed warning never to speak of family matters to strangers. That night solidified a core belief that has shadowed him ever since: he had been betrayed by the one person meant to protect him, and the world was not a place where help would arrive.

This belief system dictates the shape of his days. As an insurance agent, his work demands interaction with strangers, a constant source of low-grade terror. Before any new client meeting, Arthur performs a silent ritual, mentally reciting the makes and models of every car he has ever owned, in order. He has come to believe this mental checklist somehow neutralizes the threat, keeping the interaction contained and safe. Despite the ritual, the moment a stranger walks through the door, his body reacts as if a physical blow is imminent. He feels a familiar, humiliating lurch of panic, a response he sees as his body’s own betrayal, its stubborn refusal to acknowledge that he is no longer a helpless child. He knows his clients perceive him as aloof or distracted, and he has lost business over the years because of the invisible wall he cannot lower.

His home offers no true sanctuary. Evenings are a carefully managed exercise in distraction. The television is always on, a constant stream of noise to keep the silence—and the memories it holds—at bay. But he is vigilant about the content, quickly changing the channel at the first hint of a news report or film depicting domestic violence. He sits in his armchair, not truly watching, but listening. Every creak of the floorboards, every car that slows on the street outside, is a potential intrusion. He often finds himself reacting as if in mortal danger to the most benign sounds—the mail carrier dropping a package on the porch can trigger a full-body jolt of adrenaline that leaves him shaky for an hour. He is exhausted by this constant threat monitoring, and by the deep, abiding bitterness that the man responsible for it all died peacefully in his sleep, having faced no consequences.

What finally brought Arthur to seek help was a moment of profound loneliness. His grand-nephew had invited him to his tenth birthday party. The thought of the noisy celebration, filled with strangers—parents and children he didn't know—was so overwhelming that he declined. The image of the boy's disappointed face stayed with him for weeks. He realized then that the elaborate systems he had designed for his safety had cost him connection, joy, and family. He is afraid it may be too late to change, but a small part of him hopes to one day sit in his own home in silence and feel peace instead of peril.
